paraphrases.text: I'm not weighing in on whether student debt should be wiped out or not. My only point is that calling student loans a Ponzi scheme is wrong. A Ponzi scheme means something specific, and loans just don't fit that definition at all.

Replying to "they underestimated American industrial might": if producing more than the enemy were enough to win, the US wouldn't have lost in Vietnam or Afghanistan. Factories don't matter if nobody is willing to fight. The collapse of the Afghan army against the Taliban shows exactly that.
Cats show up in the training data. So do polar bears. The model didn't invent the idea of a cat from nothing; it saw thousands of them.

Most Christians would tell you that God does rescue people and raise them from death, just not in this life. Denominations disagree about the details of the afterlife, but salvation is central to nearly all of them.

We can let the research continue and still protect workers. A simple option is a tax on AI use: if a company cuts jobs because of AI, it pays into a fund that helps the people it let go find new work.

People are panicking about AI as if every job will disappear. Someone still has to build and run the data centres, the power grid, the renewable energy plants. Adapting to change is normal. The Industrial Revolution caused the same fear, and there were still jobs afterwards.
The only thing everyone can agree on is that the universe exists, and even that gets philosophical once you ask what existing means. Nothing gives life a meaning from outside; it makes its own.

Smash someone's camera and you'll be charged with property damage, and rightly so, whatever you think of the camera, especially if it belongs to a private person. Your argument would only hold up if you at least offered to pay the owner back.

The business decides what standard of service it wants. Good service brings customers back; bad service loses them. If staff fall short, you change their pay, retrain them or replace them. If the business is thriving and staff are still on the minimum, they can bargain for more to match what's expected of them.
I don't think that's right. Both the US and China make good economic use of what is effectively forced labour, prisoners, who are made to build furniture or farm crops that then get sold.

Funny that you're so worried about AI taking jobs when your post history is full of ChatGPT forums. Calling basic income support socialism is a stretch too. And your whole argument assumes powerful AI is coming, which isn't certain. Language models may well stay what they are: useful tools in human hands.
You don't need an economics degree to get this. Otherwise you'd be saying that raising interest rates, the standard way to fight inflation by shrinking the money supply, makes no sense.
Exactly, and student loans are no different. A family member of mine lives in luxury, is set to inherit a fortune, borrowed to study art at a private college, and has now had those loans cancelled.

Just so I understand you: the bank bailouts, the forgiven pandemic business loans, twenty years in Afghanistan, which you say nobody asked the public about. Are you claiming none of those were paid for with taxpayers' money?
Sure, most of the AI pictures are poor, but I used to pay an illustrator to draw the bags for my product. Now I don't, so I'm saving money.

Granting all of that, and granting your point that more automation is coming no matter what: isn't resisting it one way to slow things down, so that the economy and government have time to adjust? Wouldn't that soften the blow?

Except we can see, in the US especially, that wages were kept artificially low even in the good years. Producing more doesn't lower wages, it causes layoffs. That makes job hunting across every industry more competitive and lets companies hire for even less. Textbook economics ignores market manipulation, cronyism and how industries rise and fall together.

Population growth isn't even across the world. Contraception fails, sex education is poor. Everyone knows how babies are made, even in the poorest countries. And an unplanned child isn't always a disaster: there's adoption, legal guardianship, support for parents in poverty. Your argument sounds like eugenics.

Fair enough, you've changed my mind a bit: I can see there has to be some balance so that serious problems don't get out of hand. I'm still against a lot of mass surveillance, but you made some good points.

Someone else made the same point using Bigfoot, more briefly than I did. It all comes down to what we count as knowledge. I think I can fairly say I know something without being absolutely certain. Agnostic atheists seem unwilling to say they know there's no god.

Read my comment again: my point depends on the attacker supporting gun control. If they did, and gun laws had been stricter, they'd have had less reason to attack. Using a gun to kill while opposing gun access is hypocritical, but in their head it may have felt like poetic justice. I'm describing that logic, not defending it.
You asked for an example of someone wrongly locked up. I gave you one: a person jailed for a month by mistake because of a network of number plate cameras. That settles it. Have a good weekend.
A muscle you never use gets weak. The brain works the same way. Before long people will lean on AI for every small thing, stop checking facts, and just believe whatever it tells them.
Replying to "it's exactly what OP is describing": that's a caricature of Second Amendment supporters. Personally, I don't like people much, and I don't like the police hassling me either.

I'm not talking about any particular religion, just making a general point. Say there are a thousand religions. You think 999 of them are invented. I think all 1,000 are. So why does my disbelief in the 999 make sense to you, but not my disbelief in yours?

In your example the government is both the thief and the buyer, and also the consumer. A better analogy: the state takes money from the baker (private businesses) and hands it to a relative (consumers) to buy her cookies. She ends up with fewer cookies and the same money she started with. Try arguing with that.

What's your point, and what does it have to do with this? By your own logic, slavery was moral because it was accepted at the time, and trying to change something moral is immoral, so ending slavery was wrong?
Generative AI as it exists now violates creators' rights and intellectual honesty. Typing a prompt into a machine isn't making art; it's copying the work of everyone who ever shared something online.

AI is modern capitalism at its worst, and not only because the whole thing is an empty bubble. Most of the disasters AI will bring are only problems because it was built under capitalism. Blaming capitalism is fair, but it doesn't change that AI under capitalism will be behind some terrible things. All of OP's points still stand.

So what you're really saying is that in China people can criticise the government only in ways the government is free to ignore. Protesting in public and posting on a private forum are different: you can't force change by complaining where no one has to listen.

You seem to think conservatives oppose a higher minimum wage because they're cartoon villains who want everyone poor. Really they just don't want price controls, which is what a minimum wage is. Many are fine with wages rising naturally, for example if labour supply stops being flooded and pay recovers.
No, because you do use the roads. You don't use someone else's student loan. Roads are paid from taxes because everyone benefits. A degree benefits the person who got it.

This reasoning baffles me. For context, I'm an anarchist, so I'm firmly against the state taking anyone's guns; I value freedom over safety. But claiming gun control doesn't work is absurd. Japan barely has shootings, Europe has very few, and Australia cut them by about three quarters after its buyback. How is that not working?

Meh. We already get free money: lose your job and there are safety nets. A basic income just rolls all of those into one payment instead of a dozen schemes you have to chase. I honestly don't see a problem with it.

You said it's right most of the time, and that women shouldn't be seen as cruel for not wanting a child. Doesn't that mean you think there are cases where it shouldn't be allowed? Misrepresenting the other side this badly hurts your own case.

That analogy doesn't work, because in this case the 'safety rail' is the thing killing people. The proven way to stop needless deaths is to copy the countries that have neither gun violence nor authoritarian government.

Religion is plainly invented. You know it isn't real and so do I; it's stories. Nobody insists on weighing the evidence for the ancient Egyptian gods; we know they're myths, and the same goes for every religion. Most believers don't really accept the supernatural parts; they're there for the community, the music or the feeling of being right.

Maybe some god exists. But for every god anyone has actually proposed, we can see how the stories and the power structures behind them came about, which shows those religions are wrong and those gods aren't real. Why assume some other god when everything we know about the existing ones has been debunked?

Being an atheist doesn't mean being sure there are no gods. It means not believing because religion hasn't met its burden of proof. Saying "nobody knows" doesn't make unsupported religious claims as reasonable as disbelief.

Assuming companies aren't already automating wherever they can is naive. At some point the business excuses stop mattering, because people just can't afford to live. Companies need to make it work or close. Why should workers carry all the hardship?
